parameters.name: ITAM Resource Capability Level
parameters.definition: How well does the organization manage its org structure, roles, and resourcing of ITAM competencies?

rubric.level1: No dedicated ITAM roles. Asset tasks are borrowed time from the Service Desk or Procurement.
rubric.level2: ITAM roles are assigned to individuals, but they are often overwhelmed or lack formal authority to enforce policy.
rubric.level3: A formal ITAM team exists with clear job descriptions and delegated authority. Staff have ITAM-specific certifications (e.g. CHAMP, CSAM).
rubric.level4: Resource levels are data-driven. The organization measures ITAM labor hours per 1000 assets and adjusts staffing based on portfolio size.
rubric.level5: AI handles routine administrative ITAM tasks, allowing the team to focus on strategic workforce planning and high-level competency development.

parameters.name: End-User Awareness Maturity
parameters.definition: Are best practices communicated to the user community to ensure the safe and secure handling of equipment?

rubric.level1: Users receive no guidance. Equipment is treated as disposable with no sense of ownership or security responsibility.
rubric.level2: Basic Acceptable Use Policies exist in an employee handbook, but they are rarely read or promoted after the first day of work.
rubric.level3: A formal Asset Care guide is published. Regular awareness campaigns (newsletters, posters) remind users of their duties.
rubric.level4: Awareness is tested. The organization tracks User-Controllable Loss (e.g. lost chargers, cracked screens) and targets training to high-incident areas.
rubric.level5: Asset responsibility is gamified or linked to departmental sustainability goals. Users are proactive in reporting potential risks.

parameters.name: Asset Catalog Integration
parameters.definition: Does the organization use an Asset Catalogue or Preferred Asset List to standardize types (Hardware, Software, Mobile)?

rubric.level1: No standards. Users or departments buy whatever they want from any vendor, leading to a massive number of unsupportable devices.
rubric.level2: An unofficial list of preferred brands exists, but there are no technical controls to prevent non-standard purchases.
rubric.level3: A formal Asset Catalogue is published. The Procurement system is restricted to these items for 90% of all requests.
rubric.level4: The catalogue is dynamically updated. The organization measures Catalogue Compliance and the financial benefit of volume discounting via standardization.
rubric.level5: The catalogue uses AI to suggest the most energy-efficient or cost-effective models based on real-time market data and internal performance logs.

parameters.name: Discovery and Reconciliation Maturity
parameters.definition: Does the organization perform discovery vs. baseline recording and reconcile updated records against the baseline?

rubric.level1: No discovery tools. The baseline is an Excel sheet that hasn't been updated in months.
rubric.level2: Discovery tools are used occasionally (e.g. once a quarter). Discrepancies are noted but rarely fixed.
rubric.level3: Automated discovery runs weekly. A formal Reconciliation Process is triggered when the scan doesn't match the baseline.
rubric.level4: Discovery is real-time. The organization reports on Inventory Accuracy and Ghost Asset counts as a monthly KPI.
rubric.level5: The system automatically updates the asset record if a known device moves or changes specs, flagging only high-risk anomalies for human review.

parameters.name: Asset-to-ITSM Integration Level
parameters.definition: Are hardware assets integrated into the CMDB with linked relationships to Incident and Change records?

rubric.level1: Assets and the CMDB are separate silos. You cannot see which incidents are tied to which specific asset.
rubric.level2: Manual linking exists. An agent can manually type an asset tag into an incident, but there is no clickable relationship or automated mapping.
rubric.level3: The ITAM tool and CMDB share a data model. Every Incident/Change requires a linked Asset ID (CI).
rubric.level4: The organization uses the link to identify Lemon Assets (assets with high incident rates) to trigger early replacements.
rubric.level5: The asset record provides a real-time health score based on its history of Changes and Incidents, predicting when it will likely fail.

parameters.name: Supplier Integration Capability
parameters.definition: How well does the organization procure assets and related services (maintenance/consumables) across different classes?

rubric.level1: Procurement is ad-hoc and decentralized. Each department buys its own assets, often at retail prices.
rubric.level2: Centralized procurement exists for major hardware (laptops), but software and peripherals are still wild west credit card purchases.
rubric.level3: A unified procurement value stream exists for all asset classes. Underpinning contracts (UCs) are in place with preferred vendors.
rubric.level4: Procurement is Just-in-Time. The organization measures vendor lead times and Contract Value Realization (did we get the discounts we negotiated?).
rubric.level5: The procurement system is linked to vendor stock levels via API, automatically shifting orders to the fastest/cheapest partner in real-time.

parameters.name: Asset Disposal Governance Maturity
parameters.definition: Is there a formal disposal process (Hardware & Software) that includes data sanitization and partner certification?

rubric.level1: Old assets are piled in a closet or thrown in the trash. Software licenses are simply forgotten and continue to be paid for.
rubric.level2: A local recycling company picks up the hardware. No formal Certificate of Destruction is required or stored.
rubric.level3: A vetted disposal partner provides data wiping (DoD standard) and certificates for every serial number. Software licenses are formally retired.
rubric.level4: The disposal audit trail is linked to the asset record. The organization reports on Sustainable Disposal (e.g. % diverted from landfill).
rubric.level5: The organization generates revenue through secure asset remarketing and tracks the carbon footprint reduction of their disposal value stream.

parameters.name: Standardized Change Alignment
parameters.definition: Do changes to software/hardware assets follow formalized Release and Change Management processes?

rubric.level1: Users install whatever software they find. Hardware is moved between desks without any record in the Change system.
rubric.level2: Major server changes follow a process, but Standard Changes (like a RAM upgrade or a software patch) are done without updating the asset record.
rubric.level3: Any change that affects an asset's State or Configuration is captured in a formal Change record.
rubric.level4: The system flags any change detected by discovery that doesn't have a matching approved Change Request (Unauthorized Change).
rubric.level5: The system automatically blocks any asset change that would violate a license agreement or security policy.

parameters.name: ITSM Process Integration
parameters.definition: How well are AM processes aligned with other ITSM processes (Incident, Request, Change) to ensure end-to-end visibility?

rubric.level1: ITAM is isolated. Other teams don't know it exists and don't provide it with data.
rubric.level2: Occasional data sharing occurs (e.g. Service Desk sends a spreadsheet of broken laptops to ITAM once a month).
rubric.level3: ITAM triggers are built into other processes (e.g. closing a New Hire Request automatically sets the asset status to In Use).
rubric.level4: The organization measures the Velocity of the asset through the value stream (e.g. how long from Ordered to On User Desk).
rubric.level5: A single Value Stream Map defines the flow across all practices. Friction is identified and removed through cross-functional automation.

parameters.name: AM Maturity Advancement
parameters.definition: Does the organization continue to develop its AM capability towards a higher level of maturity (Continual Improvement culture)?

rubric.level1: No roadmap for improvement. Changes to the ITAM practice only happen after a crisis (e.g. a failed audit or massive budget overspend).
rubric.level2: Leadership expresses a desire to improve, but there is no formal budget or project plan dedicated to maturing the ITAM practice.
rubric.level3: A formal ITAM Maturity Roadmap is documented. The team uses ITIL 4 or ISO 19770 as a benchmark for yearly improvements.
rubric.level4: Improvement is data-driven. The organization performs Internal Gap Analysis twice a year and tracks the ROI of the ITAM practice itself.
rubric.level5: The ITAM team is a laboratory for innovation, constantly testing AI and automated FinOps strategies to stay ahead of market shifts.

parameters.name: Asset Valuation Training Maturity
parameters.definition: Is there a specialized training path for AM staff to handle Asset Valuation and demand analysis?

rubric.level1: Staff have basic technical knowledge but no training in financial management, valuation, or forecasting.
rubric.level2: Staff are sent to general ITSM or vendor training, but Financial ITAM is learned entirely on the job through trial and error.
rubric.level3: Training includes specialized certifications (e.g. CSAM, FinOps Practitioner) and internal training on the company's capital vs. operational expenditure (CAPEX/OPEX) models.
rubric.level4: Competency is tracked. Staff are audited on their ability to accurately forecast asset costs and identify under-utilized license pools.
rubric.level5: AM staff are trained to speak CFO language. They are capable of building complex business cases and financial models for multi-million dollar transformations.

parameters.name: Asset Performance Investment Index
parameters.definition: Does the organization monitor the physical health/condition and performance of assets to inform investment decisions?

rubric.level1: No health monitoring. Assets are replaced only when they break or when a user complains of slowness.
rubric.level2: Basic uptime monitoring exists for servers. For end-user devices, health is judged by age (e.g. it's 3 years old, so it must be bad).
rubric.level3: Performance telemetry (CPU, RAM, Battery health, Disk wear) is collected from the toolset and stored in the asset record.
rubric.level4: Data determines the refresh cycle. If a 4-year-old laptop has a Healthy score, its life is extended, saving capital.
rubric.level5: The system predicts when a specific model's health will drop below a usable threshold and automatically orders a replacement before the user experiences downtime.

parameters.name: Tool-Driven Demand Analysis
parameters.definition: Are the tools capable of valuating demand management options as part of project or network analysis?

rubric.level1: No valuation. Project teams guess how much hardware/software they need, often resulting in massive over-provisioning.
rubric.level2: Tools provide historical usage data, which is manually used to estimate project needs. No what-if scenario modeling.
rubric.level3: The ITAM tool allows for Demand Modeling calculating the cost impact of various scenarios (e.g. On-prem vs. Cloud vs. Hybrid).
rubric.level4: The tool provides Right-Sizing recommendations. It compares current capacity against projected demand and identifies where existing assets can be reused.
rubric.level5: The system identifies unused capacity across the network and suggests moving assets to meet new demand without new purchases.

parameters.name: Proactive Renewal Management Maturity
parameters.definition: Are renewal programs and maintenance contracts proactively managed to avoid out-of-support costs or penalty fees?

rubric.level1: Renewals are a fire drill. Management only notices a contract is ending when the vendor sends an invoice or the service gets cut off.
rubric.level2: A spreadsheet tracks expiration dates. The Renew vs. Cancel decision is made in the final 30 days, leaving no time for negotiation.
rubric.level3: A Renewal Calendar triggers a review 90-120 days in advance. Strategic vendors have quarterly business reviews (QBRs).
rubric.level4: Renewals are not automatic; they require usage data to justify the spend. The organization tracks Avoided Penalties through proactive management.
rubric.level5: The system monitors the market. If a partner's renewal price exceeds the market rate the tool triggers a Switching Feasibility analysis automatically.

parameters.name: Asset Expenditure Governance Maturity
parameters.definition: How does the organization plan and prioritize IT asset expenditure, funding, and renewal programs?

rubric.level1: Most noisy environments gets the funding. There is no formal link between ITAM data and the annual budget process.
rubric.level2: ITAM provides a list of old stuff to Finance once a year. Budgeting is based on last year + 5% rather than actual asset data.
rubric.level3: A formal Asset Investment Plan is created annually. Spending is prioritized based on risk, age, and business impact.
rubric.level4: Every dollar of asset spend must be justified by ITAM usage data. The organization measures the accuracy of spend against the plan.
rubric.level5: Budget is fluid. ITAM provides real-time Spend vs. Value insights, allowing leadership to reallocate funds mid-quarter to high-growth areas.

parameters.name: Asset Demand Forecasting Maturity
parameters.definition: How well does the organization forecast demand for services and assess the impact on its current asset portfolios?

rubric.level1: No forecasting. ITAM is purely rear-view mirror management.
rubric.level2: Some awareness of upcoming business projects exists but the impact on asset counts is calculated manually on the back of a napkin.
rubric.level3: A formal Demand-to-Asset Pipeline exists. New service launches include a Resource Impact Assessment as a mandatory step.
rubric.level4: The organization forecasts Best, Worst, and Likely demand scenarios and maps them to license and hardware availability.
rubric.level5: The system correlates external business indicators (e.g. sales pipeline, hiring plans) to automatically forecast asset demand 12 months out.

parameters.name: AM KPI & SLA Alignment
parameters.definition: Are KPIs and SLAs for the AM process appropriate and directly aligned to the organization's Service Levels?

rubric.level1: No ITAM KPIs. If they exist, they are irrelevant (e.g. number of spreadsheets updated).
rubric.level2: ITAM tracks volume (e.g. number of laptops in stock). These are not linked to the broader IT Service Levels.
rubric.level3: KPIs include Inventory Accuracy, License Compliance Ratio, and Time to Fulfill Asset Request. These are reported to IT leadership.
rubric.level4: Success is measured by Asset ROI and Cost Savings through Reharvesting. These are aligned with the CIO's corporate goals.
rubric.level5: ITAM metrics focus on Employee Productivity and Capital Efficiency. The ITAM practice is measured on its contribution to the company's profitability.

parameters.name: AM Policy & Process Alignment
parameters.definition: How well does the organization articulate its AM Policy and Objectives in alignment with the actual AM processes?

rubric.level1: There is no formal ITAM policy. Actions are taken based on individual memory or the way we've always done it.
rubric.level2: A draft policy exists but is outdated or not signed by leadership. Staff are aware of the policy but often find it contradicts real-world workflows.
rubric.level3: A formal, leadership-approved ITAM Policy is published. Objectives (e.g. 100% license compliance) are clearly linked to day-to-day procedures.
rubric.level4: Policy adherence is a KPI. Leadership receives reports on policy violations, and there is a formal mechanism to update objectives based on business changes.
rubric.level5: The ITAM policy is a core part of the Corporate Governance framework. Objectives are dynamically adjusted to meet new legal or regulatory shifts (e.g. ESG reporting).

parameters.name: Non-Compliance Risk Mitigation
parameters.definition: Is there a formal mechanism to actively limit hidden business/legal risks related to non-compliance?

rubric.level1: Risk is ignored until an audit notice or legal threat arrives. There is no understanding of hidden risks (e.g. cloud sprawl or shadow IT).
rubric.level2: The organization acknowledges risk but lacks a Risk Register. Mitigation is reactive and often expensive (e.g. paying settlement fees).
rubric.level3: A formal ITAM Risk Register is maintained. Hidden risks like License Entitlement Gaps or Software Vulnerabilities are identified and assigned owners.
rubric.level4: Risks are scored by financial impact. The organization uses Liability Exposure reports to prioritize mitigation efforts and budget allocation.
rubric.level5: AI monitors the environment to flag potential non-compliance (e.g. a developer spinning up an expensive Oracle DB) before the legal risk is realized.

parameters.name: Audit Trail & Compliance Verification
parameters.definition: Does the toolset provide a tamper-proof audit trail to support periodic verification of security and legal compliance?

rubric.level1: No audit trail. Asset records are updated by overwriting old data, making it impossible to see the who, what, when of changes.
rubric.level2: Basic logs exist but can be easily deleted or modified by administrators. Logs are rarely reviewed unless something goes wrong.
rubric.level3: The ITSM/ITAM tool maintains a systemic audit trail of all record changes. History is preserved for a defined period (e.g. 7 years) for legal reasons.
rubric.level4: The audit trail is automated and Read-Only. Regular Log Integrity checks are performed to ensure the data is reliable for external auditors.
rubric.level5: The organization uses blockchain or similar immutable logging to ensure asset history is 100% verifiable and tamper-proof for regulatory compliance.

parameters.name: Vendor Audit Management Process
parameters.definition: Are third-party vendor audits managed through a defined process that protects the organization's interests?

rubric.level1: When a vendor (e.g. Microsoft/IBM) calls for an audit, the organization scrambles, usually resulting in large unbudgeted fines.
rubric.level2: The organization cooperates with vendors but lacks its own data. They essentially take the vendor's word for what is owed.
rubric.level3: A Vendor Audit Response Protocol is in place. The organization presents its own Effective License Position (ELP) to negotiate from a position of strength.
rubric.level4: The organization performs Internal Mock Audits for top-tier vendors annually to ensure no surprises exist in the partner relationship.
rubric.level5: The organization has Pre-compliance agreements with partners where data is shared transparently via API eliminating the need for formal audits entirely.

parameters.name: ITAM Security Compliance Verification
parameters.definition: Does the organization periodically verify compliance with security requirements for all assets covered by ITAM?

rubric.level1: Asset management and Security are separate. ITAM doesn't know if an asset is patched; Security doesn't know who owns the asset.
rubric.level2: Occasional manual checks happen (e.g. do we have antivirus on these 10 laptops?). There is no schedule for full-portfolio verification.
rubric.level3: A monthly reconciliation occurs between the ITAM database and the Security Vulnerability Scanner to ensure all assets are accounted for and protected.
rubric.level4: The system flags any asset that hasn't phoned home or isn't compliant with security policies, automatically creating a high-priority incident.
rubric.level5: An asset cannot access the network unless its ITAM status is Active and its Security status is Compliant. Governance is enforced at the network level.

parameters.name: Risk-Based AM Documentation
parameters.definition: Is AM process documentation defined and implemented in accordance with a formal Risk Assessment?

rubric.level1: Documentation is non-existent or inherited from a different company. It doesn't reflect the specific risks of this organization.
rubric.level2: Basic SOPs exist, but they are generic. They don't prioritize high-risk assets (e.g. laptops with sensitive data) over low-risk ones (e.g. keyboards).
rubric.level3: Every documented process (Procurement, Disposal, Transfer) includes a Risk Control step based on a formal ITAM Risk Assessment.
rubric.level4: Documentation is updated annually. The organization measures the Effectiveness of Controls (e.g. did our disposal process successfully wipe 100% of drives?).
rubric.level5: Process documentation is linked to a Governance Risk and Compliance (GRC) tool. Changes in external law (e.g. new data privacy acts) trigger automatic updates to the SOPs.

parameters.name: AM Continuous Improvement
parameters.definition: Are AM processes regularly reviewed and improved based on audit findings and risk profiles?

rubric.level1: Processes stay the same for years regardless of how many errors or audit failures occur.
rubric.level2: Improvements are made only after a major failure. Lessons Learned are discussed but rarely lead to a formal rewrite of the process.
rubric.level3: A formal Annual Review Cycle exists for all ITAM processes. Audit findings (internal or external) are tracked to closure in the CSI Register.
rubric.level4: Improvement success is measured (e.g. the new Disposal process reduced data breach risk by 40%). This data is used to justify further ITAM investment.
rubric.level5: The practice uses a Continuous Audit model. As soon as a process bottleneck or risk is identified via data, the process is updated and redeployed in real-time.

parameters.name: Centralized ITSM Tool Standardization
parameters.definition: How do we ensure staff can accurately distinguish between incidents and requests, and are users effectively trained to report anomalies as soon as they are spotted?

rubric.level1: Users and staff are often confused between incidents and requests. Reporting is inconsistent and usually happens only when a service is completely down.
rubric.level2: Basic definitions are provided in the Service Catalog. Service Desk staff can differentiate, but end-users still report most issues via the wrong channels.
rubric.level3: Formal training programs exist for IT staff. Users have Awareness Packs that clearly define how to report anomalies. Differentiation is enforced in the tool.
rubric.level4: The organization tracks Reporting Accuracy and User-Detected vs. Tool-Detected ratios. Feedback is provided to users who incorrectly categorize tickets.
rubric.level5: Gamification and feedback loops reward users/staff for early saves (reporting something before it breaks). Detection is part of the corporate security and stability culture.

parameters.name: Monitoring-to-ITSM Integration
parameters.definition: In what ways are our monitoring tools integrated with the ITSM platform to ensure that critical alerts are automatically and accurately forwarded to the relevant Operations teams?

rubric.level1: Monitoring is siloed or non-existent. IT finds out about incidents when the phone rings.
rubric.level2: Monitors exist for Up/Down status, but alerts are sent to personal email inboxes and are often missed or ignored.
rubric.level3: Monitoring tools are integrated with the ITSM platform. Critical alerts automatically generate incident records and notify the Operations team.
rubric.level4: The system filters noise and correlates multiple events into a single incident. Detection usually happens immediately after an event occurs.
rubric.level5: AI/ML anomaly detection identifies patterns predicting an incident before it happens. The system triggers a Proactive Incident for investigation before any user impact.

parameters.name: Centralized ITSM Tool Standardization
parameters.definition: Does the organization utilize a centralized tool with standardized recording protocols to maintain data consistency across the Service Desk, Operations, and Applications teams?

rubric.level1: Teams use different methods (Excel, Email, Slack, different Jira boards) to track issues. No central view exists.
rubric.level2: Most incidents are in the ITSM tool, but Ops and App teams often work shadow tickets in their own systems without updating the central record.
rubric.level3: All teams (SD, Ops, Apps) are mandated to use the same ITSM tool. A record is created for all reported incidents without exception.
rubric.level4: The tool enforces mandatory fields for triage. Transparency is high; any stakeholder can see the real-time status of an incident across the technical stack.
rubric.level5: The tool auto-optimizes the recording workflow based on historical resolution data presenting only the most relevant fields to the specific resolver.

parameters.name: Real-time Supplier Collaboration
parameters.definition: What protocols have been established to facilitate real-time collaboration with external suppliers and ensure timely vendor notification during the detection phase?

rubric.level1: No visibility into vendor service health. IT discovers vendor outages only after internal users complain.
rubric.level2: IT staff manually check vendor Status Pages during an incident. Notifications from vendors are reactive.
rubric.level3: Formal notification protocols are in the contract. Vendors are required to alert the organization within X minutes of a detected issue.
rubric.level4: Vendor health feeds are integrated into the internal Single Pane of Glass. Alerts from vendors trigger internal incident records automatically.
rubric.level5: Shared War Rooms or ChatOps channels with vendors are permanently open. AI monitors the joint ecosystem to identify cross-provider incidents.

parameters.name: Incident Categorization & Triage
parameters.definition: What specific procedures and categorization schemes are in place to separate incidents from service requests and ensure they are prioritized correctly during triage?

rubric.level1: All tickets are handled in a single queue. Categorization is General or non-existent.
rubric.level2: Basic categories exist (Hardware/Software). Differentiation is manual. Priority is often set to High by default for all VIP users regardless of impact.
rubric.level3: A documented Priority Matrix (Urgency x Impact) and a granular Categorization Scheme are used consistently by all staff during intake.
rubric.level4: Categorization is used to drive First Contact Resolution (FCR). The organization measures Triage Accuracy and Priority Override rates.
rubric.level5: AI automatically categorizes and prioritizes incidents based on the description and historical impact data, routing them to the correct expert instantly.

parameters.name: Support Structure & Swarming
parameters.definition: How is the support structure organized across Tiered (L1/L2/L3) levels and Subject Matter Experts, and do we have the formal capability to employ swarming for complex incidents?

rubric.level1: No clear structure. Level 1 and Level 2 are often the same people. Subject matter expertise is limited and not formally mapped.
rubric.level2: A limited 2-tiered structure exists. Basic Generalists handle intake, but escalations to experts are ad-hoc and depend on who you know.
rubric.level3: A clear 3-tiered hierarchy (L1, L2, L3) is established with documented roles. SMEs are assigned to specific technology stacks.
rubric.level4: The organization measures Tier Hopping (how often a ticket moves between levels) and uses Swarming for complex cross-functional incidents.
rubric.level5: Gamification and feedback loops drive continuous learning. The structure is flexible using AI to suggest the best swarm based on real-time agent skills.

parameters.name: Incident Ownership & Escalation
parameters.definition: Who is responsible for the end-to-end ownership of an incident, and what mechanisms allow management to intervene for additional resource allocation when needed?

rubric.level1: Tickets are thrown over the fence. Once a ticket is escalated, the original agent loses sight of it. No one is truly accountable for the end-to-end fix.
rubric.level2: Incident Managers coordinate investigation for major issues, but for standard tickets, ownership is vague and depends on individual diligence.
rubric.level3: Every incident is assigned an Incident Owner at intake. This person is responsible for the resolution journey, even if they aren't the one doing the technical fix.
rubric.level4: Incident Owners have the authority to pull in senior management to unlock resources. Ownership performance is tracked as a core competency.
rubric.level5: Incident Owners act as Business Advocates, ensuring that resolution priority stays aligned with real-time business value, not just ticket age.

parameters.name: KB/KEDB Integration & Knowledge Capture
parameters.definition: Are the Knowledge Base (KB) and Known Error Database (KEDB) actively consulted during the triage phase, and is there a defined process for recording new findings back into these repositories?

rubric.level1: No formal Knowledge Base. Information sharing is informal and based on tribal knowledge or personal notes.
rubric.level2: A basic KB exists for common issues. Known Errors are documented in the tool but aren't systematically linked to new incidents.
rubric.level3: A centralized KEDB and Knowledge Base are integrated into the ITSM tool. Consultation is a mandatory step during triage and investigation.
rubric.level4: Articles include symptoms, troubleshooting steps, and workarounds. The organization measures Knowledge-Driven Resolution rates.
rubric.level5: The system uses NLP to suggest resolutions/workarounds to agents in real-time. Adaptive workflows auto-update articles based on successful resolution data.

parameters.name: Proactive Diagnostic Tool Utilization
parameters.definition: What diagnostic tools are proactively installed and utilized to ensure that critical technical data is captured before a service is restored?

rubric.level1: No diagnostic tools. Troubleshooting is guesswork or trial and error.
rubric.level2: Diagnostic data is gathered reactively after an incident occurs, often requiring a vendor to assist with log collection.
rubric.level3: A comprehensive set of diagnostic tools is identified for each technology. Staff are trained to collect and analyze data before applying a fix.
rubric.level4: Diagnostic tools are pre-installed on all core systems. The organization measures the Time to Diagnosis using these automated toolsets.
rubric.level5: The system automatically triggers diagnostic scripts the moment an anomaly is detected, presenting a pre-packaged Diagnosis Dossier to the resolver.

parameters.name: Third-Party Escalation & SLA Management
parameters.definition: How are third-party escalations managed, and do our vendor contracts include specific SLAs, priority access, or automated escalation triggers?

rubric.level1: No formal vendor interaction process. Contacts are ad-hoc or pay-per-incident without any guaranteed response time.
rubric.level2: Vendor relationships exist, but escalations are manual and lack a formal process. Vendor SLAs are not tracked against internal SLAs.
rubric.level3: Clear escalation procedures and contacts are documented for all third parties. Vendors are part of the defined escalation path.
rubric.level4: Vendor contracts include Priority Access and response SLAs. The organization measures vendor performance using the same rigor as internal teams.
rubric.level5: Real-time collaboration via shared ecosystems. Escalations to vendors occur automatically via API when specific incident triggers are met.

parameters.name: Major Incident Management (MIM) Maturity
parameters.definition: Is there a distinct process and dedicated role for Major Incident Management, and are the communication protocols clearly defined for high-priority events?

rubric.level1: No separate MIM process. Critical incidents are just big tickets handled by whoever is available.
rubric.level2: An IT manager coordinates investigation for critical issues, but communication is periodic and often distracts the technical staff from the fix.
rubric.level3: A formal, strictly adhered-to MIM process exists. A dedicated Major Incident Manager takes control of the investigation and resource coordination.
rubric.level4: Clear protocols distinguish between technical War Rooms and business-stakeholder status updates. Updates are automated and timely.
rubric.level5: The MIM process uses real-time impact visualization. Post-mortems are automated, and results are distributed to drive immediate preventative changes.

parameters.name: Incident-to-CI/RFC Linking
parameters.definition: How effectively are incidents linked to Configuration Items (CIs) and Requests for Change (RFCs), and how is the coordination of fixes managed with the Change and Release teams?

rubric.level1: Incident Management is siloed. Staff don't have access to CI details or the Change schedule.
rubric.level2: Manual linking exists. Agents might check the Change calendar to see who changed what, but there is no formal system integration.
rubric.level3: The Incident process is integrated with Configuration Management (rapid CI access) and Change Management (linking records to RFCs).
rubric.level4: The organization can trace an incident from a failed Change back to the specific CI. Fixes/workarounds are tested and approved before implementation.
rubric.level5: Automated Impact Analysis identifies which CIs and Change records are relevant to a new incident, significantly reducing Time to Repair.

parameters.name: Ticket Linking & Closure Quality
parameters.definition: What procedures govern parent-child ticket linking and backlog management, and how do we ensure user sign-off and quality monitoring occurs before final closure?

rubric.level1: Incidents are closed as soon as the agent thinks they are done. No verification or backlog tracking exists.
rubric.level2: Basic backlog tracking exists (e.g. Open ticket report). Duplicate incidents are manually identified but rarely linked.
rubric.level3: Parent-Child relationships are used to manage multiple related incidents. User sign-off is a required step before any incident is officially closed.
rubric.level4: A formal process evaluates the quality of interactions and record accuracy. The backlog is actively managed to prevent Zombie Tickets.
rubric.level5: AI validates resolution effectiveness by monitoring service health post-fix. User sign-off is gathered via seamless contextual feedback loops.

parameters.name: Incident Management Role Definition
parameters.definition: How clearly are the roles defined to distinguish between the Incident Manager's operational duties and the Process Owner's strategic oversight?

rubric.level1: No clear accountability. No one is responsible for looking at how the process actually works across the board.
rubric.level2: Incident Management roles are extra duties assigned to busy technicians. Focus is 100% on today's tickets 0% on process design.
rubric.level3: A dedicated Incident Manager oversees daily performance. An Incident Process Owner is appointed to design and integrate the process with other practices.
rubric.level4: The Process Owner is held accountable for the health of the practice (e.g. process friction adoption rates). Roles are clearly documented and reviewed annually.
rubric.level5: The Process Owner uses AI-driven insights to adjust roles and responsibilities dynamically as the business evolves or as new technology stacks are introduced.

parameters.name: Resolver Engagement & Learning
parameters.definition: What continuous training programs, feedback loops, or gamification techniques are utilized to engage resolvers and foster a culture of constant learning?

rubric.level1: No formal training. Resolvers learn by watching others. Feedback is only given when something goes wrong (Blame Culture).
rubric.level2: Standard onboarding training exists. Feedback is provided during annual performance reviews, which is too late to change behavior.
rubric.level3: Continuous training programs exist for incident and MIM teams. A No-Blame culture is fostered during post-mortems to ensure honest learning.
rubric.level4: Individual performance data is shared with resolvers. Gamification (e.g. leaderboards for KB contributions) encourages positive behavior.
rubric.level5: Adaptive feedback loops use AI to suggest personalized training modules to resolvers based on their specific resolution history and skill gaps.

parameters.name: Predictive Analytics & Automated RCA
parameters.definition: To what extent are we leveraging predictive analytics and automated root cause analysis (RCA) to identify and report on recurring incident trends?

rubric.level1: No trend analysis. Each incident is treated as a new, isolated event even if it happened yesterday.
rubric.level2: Basic monthly reports show Top 10 Incident Categories. Manual review is required to see if they are related.
rubric.level3: The toolset performs trend analysis to identify recurring issues, which are then manually promoted to the Problem Management practice.
rubric.level4: Automated Root Cause Analysis (RCA) tools identify clusters of incidents in real-time. The system measures the Time to Identify Trends.
rubric.level5: AI-powered analytics dynamically recommend process improvements. The system auto-identifies at-risk services before they fail based on historical trends.

parameters.name: Partner Participation in PIRs
parameters.definition: How effectively do our external partners participate in Post-Incident Reviews (PIRs), and what is the process for auditing their performance against established SLAs and OLAs?

rubric.level1: Suppliers are ignored during improvement cycles. If they fail, IT just complains without data.
rubric.level2: Supplier SLAs are monitored. Performance is discussed during contract renewals, but not on a monthly operational basis.
rubric.level3: Suppliers are required to participate in Post-Incident Reviews (PIRs) for incidents involving their services. Monthly performance reviews are documented.
rubric.level4: Joint CSI Initiatives are launched with key partners to reduce incident volumes at the source. Partner data is integrated into the internal CSI register.
rubric.level5: Performance data is shared in real-time. Multi-vendor post-mortems use a shared data environment to identify ecosystem-wide improvements.

parameters.name: Post-Mortem & Knowledge Redistribution
parameters.definition: Are formal post-mortems conducted for all critical incidents, and is there a structured workflow to ensure findings are redistributed into Updated KB articles and SOPs?

rubric.level1: No post-mortems. When a major incident ends, everyone goes back to work and hopes it doesn't happen again.
rubric.level2: Informal debriefs occur after a Major incident. Some notes are taken, but they are rarely turned into actionable changes.
rubric.level3: Formal PIRs are mandatory for all critical incidents. Results are documented, distributed, and used to update Knowledge Base articles and SOPs.
rubric.level4: The organization tracks the completion of Preventative Actions identified in PIRs. Success is measured by the lack of repeat critical incidents.
rubric.level5: The PIR process is automated where possible (data gathering). High-priority findings trigger automated workflow updates to prevent recurrence instantly.

parameters.name: CSAT Tracking & Quality Monitoring
parameters.definition: What mechanisms are in place to track Customer Satisfaction (CSAT) and monitor the overall quality of both technical records and user interactions?

rubric.level1: No quality checks. CSAT is only measured if a user sends a complaint email.
rubric.level2: Random ticket audits occur. Passive CSAT surveys are sent after closure, but response rates are low (<5%) and results are ignored.
rubric.level3: A formal Quality Monitoring process evaluates the accuracy of records and the quality of user interactions. CSAT is a key parameter for the practice.
rubric.level4: The organization uses AI to analyze the Tone and Satisfaction of interactions across all channels. Quality scores are linked to resolver performance.
rubric.level5: Customer feedback is used to drive Persona-based process improvements. Real-time satisfaction levels influence how incidents are routed and prioritized.

parameters.name: Incident Management CSI Integration
parameters.definition: How is the Incident Management practice integrated into the CSI program to identify process deficiencies and ensure the organization consistently meets its SLA, SLO, and availability targets?

rubric.level1: No CSI program. The Incident process hasn't changed in years.
rubric.level2: Managers recognize we could do better, but there is no list of improvements or budget to execute them.
rubric.level3: A formal CSI Register exists for Incident Management. Performance is measured against SLAs and SLOs, and gaps trigger improvement projects.
rubric.level4: Incidents are monitored and escalated when SLOs are in danger of being breached. Improvement projects are prioritized by their impact on Business Availability.
rubric.level5: The practice uses Lean techniques to remove waste. Improvements are deployed in small, frequent cycles, and the Success of the Improvement is measured via data.

parameters.name: Problem Management Accountability
parameters.definition: How is accountability clearly split between the Problem Manager and Problem Owner, and what training or Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) ensure consistent execution?

rubric.level1: No dedicated roles. Problem management is everyone's job and no one's job. No SOP exists.
rubric.level2: Problem tasks are assigned as extra duties to support staff. A basic SOP exists but is rarely followed.
rubric.level3: A designated Problem Manager (Process) and Problem Owners (Investigation) are in place. All staff are trained on a documented SOP
rubric.level4: Job descriptions explicitly include PM responsibilities. Training effectiveness is measured by the quality and accuracy of investigation records.
rubric.level5: Roles are agile; the organization uses Skills Matrices to automatically assign Problem Owners based on the specific technical failure pattern.

parameters.name: AI/ML-Driven Problem Identification
parameters.definition: How effectively are we leveraging AI/ML, trend analysis, and ITSM tool integration across incidents and events to identify underlying problems?

rubric.level1: No tools for trend analysis. Problems are identified manually when someone notices this keeps happening.
rubric.level2: The tool supports basic logging and categorization. Manual reports are generated monthly to look for recurring incidents.
rubric.level3: Tooling facilitates automated impact/urgency assignment and links Incidents to Problems. Regular trend analysis is a manual but scheduled process.
rubric.level4: The tool integrates with the CMS/CMDB and Event Monitoring. It automatically flags Problem Candidates based on recurring patterns or event clusters.
rubric.level5: AI/ML-assisted identification uses historical data to predict potential failures. The system proactively creates problem records before a major incident occurs.

parameters.name: Standardized Problem Logging
parameters.definition: Are problem records logged using standardized formats that align with Service Desk categories, and how is the impact assessment conducted to determine priority?

rubric.level1: Problem logging is ad-hoc. Categories don't match Incident Management, making it impossible to correlate data.
rubric.level2: Problems are logged for major incidents, but categorization is inconsistent and lacks granularity.
rubric.level3: Logging is a formal requirement. Problem categorization is fully compatible with Service Desk categories. A documented Priority Scheme (Impact x Urgency) is strictly used.
rubric.level4: Categorization is used to identify High-Risk technology areas. The organization measures the Accuracy of Initial Impact Assessment against final results.
rubric.level5: Continuous improvement processes regularly update categorization and logging standards based on shifts in the infrastructure and business needs.

parameters.name: Formal RCA Methodologies & Tools
parameters.definition: Which formal RCA methodologies such as the 5 Whys or data-driven brainstorming are utilized alongside diagnostic tools to identify the source of failures?

rubric.level1: RCA is educated guessing. No formal method is used.
rubric.level2: RCA is performed via brainstorming sessions. Findings are based on memory and process of elimination rather than hard data.
rubric.level3: Systematic methods (e.g. 5 Whys, Ishikawa/Fishbone) are applied. Diagnostic data is gathered while incidents are occurring for later analysis.
rubric.level4: RCA is driven by deep log analysis and technical experts. Findings are validated by re-creating the issue in a controlled environment.
rubric.level5: The system implements automated correlation and impact prediction tools. AI provides a Root Cause Dossier by correlating cross-stack logs instantly upon problem creation.

parameters.name: Auto-Remediation & Stability Validation
parameters.definition: What capabilities exist for deploying auto-remediation scripts, and how is infrastructure monitoring used to validate the stability of a service post-resolution?

rubric.level1: All fixes are manual and ad-hoc. No testing is performed.
rubric.level2: Some manual scripts are used to fix issues, but they aren't stored centrally or maintained.
rubric.level3: Fixes are formally tested and submitted via Change Management. Infrastructure is monitored after resolution to ensure stability.
rubric.level4: A library of approved fixes exists. Successful resolutions are measured against quality criteria (fix durability/recurrence rates).
rubric.level5: Auto-remediation scripts are triggered automatically by known patterns. The system monitors for regressions and auto-reverts if a fix introduces new issues.

parameters.name: Supplier Collaboration for Problems
parameters.definition: What formalized protocols are in place to ensure seamless collaboration with third-party suppliers when resolving complex, cross-platform problems?

rubric.level1: Vendors are only contacted if a component is broken. No shared problem-solving occurs.
rubric.level2: Vendors are engaged for complex issues, but there is no formal process or defined contact list.
rubric.level3: Vendor collaboration processes for diagnostics are defined. Escalation paths for complex investigations are documented in contracts.
rubric.level4: Vendors are part of Problem Review meetings. Performance is tracked regarding the Time to Provide Root Cause.
rubric.level5: Real-time diagnostic data sharing with external suppliers. The organization and vendor operate in a Shared Problem Backlog for critical technology stacks.

parameters.name: KEDB Maintenance & Workarounds
parameters.definition: How is the Known Error Database (KEDB) maintained, and what is the specific workflow for communicating workarounds to the Service Desk and triggering RFCs for permanent fixes?

rubric.level1: Known errors are not recorded. Workarounds are passed by word-of-mouth.
rubric.level2: A list of known errors exists in a folder. The Service Desk might be told about a workaround if they ask.
rubric.level3: A formal KEDB is maintained. Workarounds are proactively communicated to the Service Desk and documented as knowledge articles. RFCs are raised for all permanent fixes.
rubric.level4: Every Problem record must have a validated workaround or an approved plan if no fix is found. Workaround effectiveness is tracked via Incident Re-open rates.
rubric.level5: The KEDB is fully integrated with Incident Management (auto-suggest). Lessons learned from major problems are automatically fed into the Continual Improvement program.

parameters.name: Supplier Problem Governance
parameters.definition: What KPIs and governance structures, including post-mortems and executive reporting, are used to drive the continual improvement of the Problem Management practice?

rubric.level1: No Problem Management metrics. Success is no major outages today.
rubric.level2: Basic metrics (number of open problems) are reported occasionally.
rubric.level3: KPIs and SLAs for PM are defined and tracked. Post-mortems are conducted for all major problems and results are reported to management.
rubric.level4: Client satisfaction (CSAT) with problem resolution is tracked. Metrics focus on Reduction in Recurring Incidents and Fix Quality.
rubric.level5: Problem data is shared with Service Level Management to influence business strategy. Predictive analytics are used to recommend process improvements dynamically.

parameters.name: Change Management Roles & CAB
parameters.definition: How clearly defined are the roles of the Change Owner and Manager, and how do the CAB and ECAB structures ensure that Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) are appropriately involved in the approval process?

rubric.level1: No designated Change Manager. Roles are ad-hoc, and it's unclear who has the authority to approve a change.
rubric.level2: Roles are assigned, but the Change Manager acts mostly as a coordinator without the authority to enforce policy.
rubric.level3: Change Manager and CAB/ECAB are formally established. Roles for SMEs and Business Representatives (BRM/SDM) are documented and followed.
rubric.level4: Change Authorities are delegated based on risk levels. The effectiveness of the CAB is measured by Lead Time and Approval Accuracy.
rubric.level5: The Change Authority is dynamic. AI suggests the best Virtual CAB for specific technical changes based on historical success and expertise.

parameters.name: Standard Change Automation
parameters.definition: To what extent are standard changes automated within the service lifecycle, and how does our ITSM tooling facilitate the efficient creation and assignment of Request for Change (RFC) forms?

rubric.level1: RFCs are handled via email or paper. No tool supports categorization or workflow.
rubric.level2: A basic tool is used to log RFCs. It provides a simple repository but does not enforce a specific workflow for different change types.
rubric.level3: A centralized ITSM tool is used by all IT areas. It supports specific workflows for Normal, Standard, and Emergency changes.
rubric.level4: Low-risk standard changes are 100% automated. The tool provides a Projected Service Outage (PSO) view for all stakeholders.
rubric.level5: AI-driven failure prediction and proactive risk mitigation are built into the tool. Predictive analytics forecast change timelines and success rates.

parameters.name: Change Categorization SOPs
parameters.definition: Are there formalized Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that govern the categorization of changes specifically distinguishing between Normal, Standard, and Emergency types?

rubric.level1: No standard process. Every change is handled differently. Emergency is used for everything to bypass the queue.
rubric.level2: A basic process exists. RFCs have some standard info, but filtering of incomplete requests is inconsistent.
rubric.level3: A formal SOP defines the full lifecycle. Standard changes are strictly defined as repeatable/low-risk, and Emergency changes are limited to critical incidents.
rubric.level4: Process performance is tracked. RFC forms include business priority and desired implementation dates, which drive the Change Schedule.
rubric.level5: The Change SOP is a living document, updated automatically via feedback loops. Processes auto-optimize based on historical resolution and implementation data.

parameters.name: Change Communication & Peer Review
parameters.definition: What communication plans are in place to ensure stakeholders and end-users are aware of potential disruptions, and how is a peer review culture promoted to mitigate risk?

rubric.level1: IT changes happen in a vacuum. Users are surprised by outages, and there is no formal communication plan for stakeholders.
rubric.level2: Communication is ad-hoc (e.g. a global email sent 10 minutes before a change). Some technical staff perform informal peer reviews.
rubric.level3: Stakeholder engagement and communication plans are mandatory for all Normal changes. The organization is fully aware of the disruptive potential of changes.
rubric.level4: AI-driven sentiment analysis measures change adoption and satisfaction. Feedback is gathered from customers to ensure changes support business needs.
rubric.level5: Real-time status tracking provides 100% transparency. Business stakeholders are active participants in joint training and risk mitigation sessions.

parameters.name: Collision Detection & Unauthorized Change
parameters.definition: How effectively do we utilize CMDB integration and collision detection tools to predict failures and identify unauthorized changes that may have bypassed the formal process?

rubric.level1: Impact analysis is based on the memory of the technician. No technical detection for unauthorized changes exists.
rubric.level2: The tool provides basic risk fields (High/Med/Low), but impact analysis is manual. Unauthorized changes are only found if they cause an outage.
rubric.level3: Impact analysis is integrated with the CMDB to determine dependencies. Technical solutions are in place to detect and flag unauthorized changes.
rubric.level4: Automated compliance validation is in place. The toolset uses historical data to predict failure probability and automatically detects Collisions (overlapping changes).
rubric.level5: AI/ML failure prediction and proactive risk mitigation are standard. The system automatically blocks high-risk changes that lack a validated rollback plan.

parameters.name: Joint Supplier Impact Assessment
parameters.definition: What protocols exist for conducting joint impact assessments with external suppliers, and how is the coordination of execution managed for supplier-led changes?

rubric.level1: Vendor changes (e.g. SaaS updates) happen without the organization's knowledge. No vendor SLAs for changes exist.
rubric.level2: Vendors notify the team of changes but the internal team doesn't assess the risk to integrated internal systems.
rubric.level3: Risk evaluation of supplier-led changes and third-party integrations is mandatory. Defined SLAs with suppliers for external service changes are in place.
rubric.level4: Joint change impact assessments are conducted with external vendors. Real-time coordination occurs for all third-party change executions.
rubric.level5: Contractual governance frameworks ensure suppliers are 100% aligned with internal change policies. Integrated AI monitors the entire supplier ecosystem for change risks.

parameters.name: Impact Assessment & Rollback Planning
parameters.definition: What formal methodologies are used to assess Business, Technical, and SLA impacts, and is a robust back-out (rollback) plan mandated for every change?

rubric.level1: No formal risk assessment. Back-out plans are rarely created and almost never tested. PIRs are only done for disasters.
rubric.level2: Basic risk ratings (H/M/L) are assigned. A Back-out section exists on the form but is often filled with reboot server or restore from backup without detail.
rubric.level3: Detailed Business, Technical, and SLA impact assessments are mandatory. Back-out plans are created and tested for every change.
rubric.level4: All changes are subject to a Post-Implementation Review (PIR). Unauthorized changes are reviewed by the CAB for root cause analysis.
rubric.level5: Automated rollback and contingency planning for high-risk changes. Lessons learned from all changes (successful and failed) auto-feed into process improvements.

parameters.name: Change Governance Accountability
parameters.definition: How does management demonstrate accountability for governance, and what measures ensure that all staff remain aware of change policies and their specific role assignments?

rubric.level1: No designated owner for governance. Staff are unaware of their roles in the change process and policies are not documented.
rubric.level2: A process owner is named, but they lack the authority to enforce policies. Responsibilities are assigned but often conflict with other duties.
rubric.level3: A designated Change Process Owner is responsible for governance. Roles and responsibilities are formally documented, assigned, and clearly communicated across IT.
rubric.level4: Change management policies are actively enforced. The organization tracks Role Competency and ensures that those performing changes are certified/trained on the SOP.
rubric.level5: Governance is integrated into the corporate culture. AI-driven feedback loops ensure that roles are dynamically adjusted to maintain the highest compliance standards.

parameters.name: Immutable Audit Trails & Compliance
parameters.definition: Are we leveraging immutable audit trails and automated compliance validation to ensure technical safeguards are met and that audit reporting is seamless?

rubric.level1: No audit trail exists. Compliance is checked manually (and rarely). There is no technical way to detect if a change happened without an RFC.
rubric.level2: The tool logs basic changes, but logs can be altered by admins. Compliance reports are manual snapshot exports in Excel.
rubric.level3: The tool provides a systematic audit trail. Automated compliance validation is in place for regulated changes. Technical solutions scan for unauthorized changes.
rubric.level4: The toolset provides an Immutable Audit Trail (tamper-proof). Automated audit reporting is generated in real-time, highlighting policy deviations immediately.
rubric.level5: AI-driven compliance risk assessments and proactive issue resolution are standard. The system automatically blocks any deployment that fails the automated compliance check.

parameters.name: Third-Party Governance & Contracts
parameters.definition: How are supplier compliance assessments integrated into our governance framework to ensure their activities align perfectly with our internal change policies?

rubric.level1: No oversight of vendor-managed changes. It is assumed the supplier follows the rules, but no evidence is ever requested.
rubric.level2: Vendors provide their own change reports, but these are not audited against the organization's internal standards.
rubric.level3: Contractual governance frameworks ensure suppliers are aligned with internal change policies. Third-party compliance assessments are conducted regularly.
rubric.level4: Real-time tracking of vendor-managed changes is integrated into the internal dashboard. Suppliers are audited against specific regulatory and security KPIs.
rubric.level5: The organization and its suppliers operate in a unified governance framework. Automated cross-entity compliance validation ensures 100% policy adherence.

parameters.name: Policy Enforcement & Continuity
parameters.definition: How are change policies integrated with Service Continuity and contingency plans to ensure that regulatory and security requirements are monitored and enforced throughout the process?

rubric.level1: Policies are suggestions and frequently bypassed. There is no link between Change and Service Continuity/Recovery plans.
rubric.level2: A Change Policy exists but is not strictly enforced. Information is occasionally shared with Problem Management but not on a structured basis.
rubric.level3: A formalized Change Policy and SOP are actively enforced. Change Management routinely collaborates with Configuration, Problem, and Service Continuity teams.
rubric.level4: A formalized Change Policy and SOP are actively enforced. Change Management routinely collaborates with Configuration, Problem, and Service Continuity teams.
rubric.level5: The process is compliant by design. Continuous tracking of policy adherence and regulatory requirements is automated, with the value stream auto-adjusting to new laws.

parameters.name: IT Systems, Data Center & Technology
parameters.definition: Readiness of IT infrastructure, platforms, and DR site capabilities to support system recovery during a disaster.

rubric.level1: No dedicated DR infrastructure, recovery depends on rebuilding systems manually on available resources.
rubric.level2: Basic DR setup exists (e.g. backups or limited standby systems), but capacity and readiness are not sufficient for full recovery.
rubric.level3: DR environment is established for critical systems, infrastructure and replication are configured but not fully validated.
rubric.level4: DR infrastructure is sized and maintained to support critical workloads, replication and failover capabilities are regularly tested.
rubric.level5: DR infrastructure is robust and scalable, systems can be recovered reliably across sites with minimal disruption.

parameters.name: Recovery Time Objectives
parameters.definition: Maximum acceptable time to restore a system or application after a disruption

rubric.level1: RTO is not defined, recovery timelines are unpredictable and depend on manual effort.
rubric.level2: Basic RTO targets exist for a few critical systems, but are not consistently achieved.
rubric.level3: RTO is defined per application, recovery procedures are documented but execution varies.
rubric.level4: RTO targets are consistently met for critical systems through tested DR processes.
rubric.level5: Recovery is streamlined with automated failover, RTO is minimized and consistently achieved across workloads.

parameters.name: Recovery Point Objectives
parameters.definition: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.

rubric.level1: RPO is not defined, data loss during failure is unpredictable.
rubric.level2: Basic RPO targets exist for a few critical systems, but backups are infrequent and inconsistent.
rubric.level3: RPO is defined per application, backup/replication schedules are aligned but not always met.
rubric.level4: RPO targets are consistently achieved using regular backups or replication for critical systems.
rubric.level5: Near real-time data protection for critical workloads, minimal data loss with continuous or frequent replication.

parameters.name: Data backup
parameters.definition: Availability and accessibility of backup data during a disaster for successful recovery.

rubric.level1: Backups may exist but are not readily accessible during a disaster, recovery is uncertain.
rubric.level2: Backups are available for some critical systems but may require manual effort or delays to access.
rubric.level3: Backups are available for most critical workloads and can be accessed within defined procedures.
rubric.level4: Backup data is consistently available and accessible within defined RTO/RPO requirements, including offsite storage.
rubric.level5: Backup data is readily accessible across locations (e.g. DR site/cloud) with minimal delay, supporting reliable recovery for most workloads.

parameters.name: System Failover/Failback capability
parameters.definition: Ability to switch operations to a DR environment (failover) and return to primary site (failback) with minimal disruption.

rubric.level1: No defined failover or failback process, recovery is manual and unstructured.
rubric.level2: Basic failover possible for a few systems, but largely manual, failback process is unclear or untested.
rubric.level3: Failover and failback procedures are documented, partial execution possible but requires manual coordination.
rubric.level4: Failover and failback are tested and can be executed within defined RTO, processes are standardized for critical systems.
rubric.level5: Failover and failback are streamlined with minimal manual effort, regularly tested and reliable across critical workloads.

parameters.name: Documentation
parameters.definition: Availability, accuracy, and usability of documented DR plans, procedures, and dependencies.

rubric.level1: No formal DR documentation, recovery depends on individual knowledge.
rubric.level2: Basic DR documents exist for some systems, but are incomplete, outdated, or not easily accessible.
rubric.level3: DR procedures are documented for critical systems, documents are available but not regularly updated.
rubric.level4: Comprehensive DR documentation is maintained, regularly updated, and aligned with current infrastructure and processes.
rubric.level5: DR documentation is standardized, version-controlled, easily accessible, and validated through regular DR testing and audits.

parameters.name: Risk Management
parameters.definition: Identification, assessment, and mitigation of risks that could impact business continuity.

rubric.level1: No formal risk assessment, risks are addressed only after incidents occur.
rubric.level2: Basic risk identification performed for some areas, assessments are informal and not regularly updated.
rubric.level3: Structured risk assessment process exists, key risks are documented and periodically reviewed.
rubric.level4: Comprehensive risk assessments are conducted regularly, mitigation plans are defined and tracked.
rubric.level5: Risk management is integrated into business processes with continuous monitoring and regular updates aligned to business changes.

parameters.name: Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
parameters.definition: Process of identifying critical business functions, dependencies, and the impact of disruptions (including RTO/RPO requirements).

rubric.level1: No formal BIA performed, critical business functions and impacts are not clearly understood.
rubric.level2: Basic BIA conducted for a few critical functions, lacks consistency and is not regularly updated.
rubric.level3: Structured BIA completed for key business units, critical functions, dependencies, and RTO/RPO are documented.
rubric.level4: Comprehensive BIA covering all major business functions, reviewed periodically and aligned with business priorities.
rubric.level5: BIA is regularly updated and integrated into planning, used to drive DR/BC strategies and investment decisions.

parameters.name: Communication plans
parameters.definition: Defined processes for internal and external communication during a disruption, including roles, escalation paths, and stakeholders.

rubric.level1: No formal communication plan, coordination happens informally during incidents.
rubric.level2: Basic contact lists exist, but roles, escalation paths, and communication methods are unclear.
rubric.level3: Communication plan is documented with defined roles, contact lists, and escalation procedures.
rubric.level4: Communication plans are regularly updated, tested during drills, and include internal and external stakeholders.
rubric.level5: Communication is well-coordinated and timely during incidents, plans are integrated with crisis management and continuously improved.

parameters.name: Continuity strategies
parameters.definition: Defined approaches to maintain or quickly resume critical business operations during disruptions (e.g. alternate sites, remote work, manual workarounds, DR alignment).

rubric.level1: No defined continuity strategies, business relies on reactive decisions during disruptions.
rubric.level2: Basic strategies exist for a few critical functions (e.g. manual workarounds), but are not formalized or consistent.
rubric.level3: Continuity strategies are documented for key business functions, aligned with BIA, but not fully tested.
rubric.level4: Strategies are implemented, tested, and aligned with DR capabilities, alternate arrangements (sites, resources) are in place.
rubric.level5: Continuity strategies are regularly validated, adaptable to different scenarios, and integrated into overall business operations.

parameters.name: People & Process
parameters.definition: Readiness of personnel, roles, responsibilities, and operational processes to support business continuity during disruptions.

rubric.level1: No defined roles or processes, response depends on individual effort and availability.
rubric.level2: Basic roles are identified for key personnel, but responsibilities and processes are unclear or inconsistent.
rubric.level3: Roles and responsibilities are documented, continuity processes are defined but not consistently practiced.
rubric.level4: Teams are trained on their roles, processes are tested through drills and followed during incidents.
rubric.level5: Roles and processes are well understood across teams, regular training and improvements ensure consistent and effective response
